title: Multilingual & Culturally-Adapted Materials
section: What you’ll be able to do
text:
What you’ll be able to do

Translate outreach materials into another language with AI
Adapt for cultural context, not just words
Quality-check with back-translation and a human reviewer

title: Multilingual & Culturally-Adapted Materials
text:
Overview
AI translates quickly and can adapt tone for a community, but machine translation makes confident errors — especially with idioms, health terms, and culturally specific concepts. A human speaker should review anything that reaches the public.
Cultural adaptation is more than translation: examples, framing, and imagery may need to change. AI can propose options; community knowledge decides.

title: Multilingual & Culturally-Adapted Materials
text:
Practice activities
Activity 1 · Moderate — Translate with back-translation QA
Time ~15 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu (or an approved translation tool)
Goal. Translate an outreach message and catch errors before it goes public.
Setup. Use this pedestrian-safety outreach message and translate it into Spanish (the most common non-English language in Philadelphia):

Walk Safely in Your Neighborhood
Pedestrian crashes in Philadelphia peak between 4 and 7 PM, especially on wide, busy roads. Here’s how to stay safer:

Cross at marked crosswalks and intersections — drivers are more likely to see you there.
Make eye contact with drivers before stepping into the street.
At night, wear something light-colored or reflective. Carry a flashlight if you can.
If there’s no sidewalk, walk facing traffic so you can see oncoming cars.
Report broken streetlights, missing crosswalk markings, or damaged sidewalks to 311 (call 311 or use the Philly311 app).

Your safety matters. If a street in your neighborhood feels dangerous to walk on, you can request a traffic-safety review from the city at [link].

Steps.

Translate:

Translate this community health message into [language], keeping a warm, plain-language tone. [message]

In a fresh chat, back-translate:

Translate this [language] text back into English, literally. [translation]

Compare the back-translation to your original and investigate any drift in meaning.

Expected result. A translation plus a back-translation you’ve compared.
Check your work. A bilingual colleague should review anything published — machine translation of health terms is error-prone.
Common pitfalls. Idioms and clinical terms mistranslate confidently. Never publish machine translation of health materials unreviewed.
Stretch (optional). Ask which sentences are most likely to be misunderstood in the target language.

Activity 2 · Moderate — Culturally adapt, not just translate
Time ~13 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu
Goal. Adapt framing and examples for a specific community, not just the words.
Setup. Your Spanish translation from Activity 1, plus this community context: the target audience is Spanish-speaking residents of North Philadelphia, many of whom are originally from Puerto Rico or the Dominican Republic. The neighborhood has high pedestrian crash rates, limited sidewalk infrastructure, and several schools within walking distance.
Steps.

Surface adaptation needs:

For [community], how might the examples, framing, or imagery in this message land differently? Suggest culturally appropriate adaptations. [message + community]

Draft an adapted version; mark what a community reviewer must confirm.
Check for harm:

Flag anything in my adaptation that could unintentionally stereotype or exclude.


Expected result. An adapted draft plus a list to verify with community members.
Check your work. Cultural knowledge belongs to the community — AI suggestions are hypotheses to confirm, not facts.
Common pitfalls. AI can introduce stereotypes while “adapting.” Review with people from the community.
Stretch (optional). Make two variants and plan a quick community feedback check.

Activity 3 · Moderate — Scale translation QA across languages with Claude Cowork
Time ~20 min · Tools Claude Cowork (consumer/PI-purchased — not Drexel-supported; Low Risk Data only)
Goal. Run the same translate-then-back-translate QA check from Activity 1 across three languages at once, the way a real multilingual campaign actually goes out.
Setup. Real outreach rarely ships in one language. Spanish is Philadelphia’s most common non-English language, but DSPH projects often also need Vietnamese, Chinese, or others — and each version needs the same QA check. Instead of re-prompting a chat window three times, connect a folder and let Cowork work across all the files at once. Create a folder containing one file, original-message.txt, with the same pedestrian-safety message from Activity 1 (it’s already public and non-sensitive — keep it that way; nothing above Low Risk goes into Cowork). Connect that folder to a Cowork session.
Steps.

Ask Cowork to translate into all three languages, one file per language:

In the connected folder, read original-message.txt. Translate it into Spanish, Vietnamese, and Simplified Chinese, keeping a warm, plain-language tone. Save each as translation-[language].txt — three separate files.

Then have it back-translate each one, as literally as possible:

Now back-translate each translation-[language].txt into English, as literally as possible, without looking at the original. Save each as backtranslation-[language].txt.

Finally, ask for a single consolidated QA table:

Compare each back-translation against original-message.txt. Create qa-report.md with a table: one row per language, columns for sentences that drifted in meaning, the nature of the drift (idiom, health term, tone), and a severity flag. Flag any language where meaning shifted.

Open the folder: you should have three translations, three back-translations, and one QA report. Read the flagged rows and spot-check them against the files.

Expected result. Seven files — one original, three translations, three back-translations — plus a consolidated QA table telling you where to look first in each language.
Check your work. The QA table is a triage step, not a sign-off. A bilingual human must review each language’s version before anything is published — same rule as Activity 1, now times three.
Common pitfalls. The same model translating and grading itself can miss its own confident errors — that’s exactly why the human review rule doesn’t scale away. And remember Cowork’s data status: Low Risk (public) content only, unless separately approved.
Stretch (optional). Ask Cowork to add a column to the QA table noting reading level per translation, and whether any language’s version drifted above plain-language level.

title: Qualitative Data Analysis
section: What you’ll be able to do
text:
What you’ll be able to do

Use AI to propose codes and group themes in open-text data
Build and apply a codebook, then verify agreement
Weigh the debate over AI in qualitative work and protect confidentiality

title: Qualitative Data Analysis
text:
Overview
AI can suggest codes, group themes, and summarize patterns in interview or open-text data quickly. But qualitative scholars warn that outsourcing interpretation strips out the reflexivity that gives the method its meaning. Use AI to assist your reading, not replace it.
Transcripts are often sensitive. De-identify them and use an approved tool — confidentiality comes first.

title: Qualitative Data Analysis
text:
Practice activities
Activity 1 · Moderate — Draft a codebook from open-text
Time ~18 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu (approved tool for this content)
Goal. Build a codebook from qualitative responses while keeping your interpretation central.
Setup. Use a small, non-sensitive set of open-ended responses. You can use the free-text “description” field from a 311 Service & Information Requests slice, or the eight sample walkability comments below:

“Cars fly down our street, no stop signs.” · “Sidewalks are cracked and hard with a stroller.” · “I feel safe walking to the train in the morning.” · “No crosswalk near the school, kids dart across.” · “Too dark at night, the lights are out.” · “Love the new bump-outs, easier to cross.” · “Trash and parked cars block the corner.” · “The bus stop has nowhere to sit or shelter.”

Steps.

Draft a codebook:

Propose an initial qualitative codebook for these walkability comments: 5–7 codes, each with a name, a one-sentence definition, and an example quote. Note any response that could fit more than one code.

Revise with your own judgment — rename, merge, or split codes. You own the meaning.
Apply it back:

Using my revised codebook, code each comment and show your reasoning for each.


Expected result. A codebook (codes + definitions + examples) that you have revised.
Check your work. Do the codes capture what respondents meant, or just what was easy to label? Adjust accordingly.
Common pitfalls. AI flattens nuance and imposes its own frame — treat it as a first pass, not the analysis. De-identify any real transcripts and use an approved tool.
Stretch (optional). Ask AI to surface a theme across codes, then find a quote that complicates that theme.

Activity 2 · Moderate — Code a new batch and check agreement
Time ~13 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu
Goal. Apply the codebook and check reliability against your own coding.
Setup. Use this second batch of 8 walkability comments (different from Activity 1):

“The new bike lane is great but now there’s nowhere to load groceries.” · “My wheelchair can’t get over the curb at 5th and Spring Garden.” · “Drivers run the red at Broad and Lehigh every single day.” · “We need more benches — older people can’t walk far without resting.” · “The crossing signal doesn’t last long enough to get across safely.” · “I’d walk to work but there’s no sidewalk on the last two blocks.” · “The school zone signs are hidden behind a tree branch.” · “I feel safer since they added the speed bumps on my block.”

Steps.

Have AI code them:

Using this codebook, code each of these new responses and show which code(s) apply and why.

Independently code the same eight yourself.
Compare:

Here is the AI’s coding and mine. Where do we disagree, and what’s the likely reason?


Expected result. A coded batch plus a short list of disagreements.
Check your work. Disagreements should point to fuzzy code definitions — tighten them.
Common pitfalls. High agreement can be false comfort if the codebook is shallow. Your reading is the standard, not the AI’s.
Stretch (optional). Refine the codebook from the disagreements and re-run the batch.

Activity 3 · Moderate — Apply Your Codebook Across Multiple Files with Claude Cowork
Time ~20 min · Tools Claude Cowork
Goal. Apply the codebook you built in Activities 1–2 consistently across both batches of walkability comments stored as separate files — the way real qualitative data actually arrives — while keeping every interpretive decision yourself.
Setup. Create a folder on your computer called walkability-coding. Save Batch 1’s eight comments as batch1.txt (one comment per line) and Batch 2’s eight comments as batch2.txt. Add a third file, codebook.txt, containing your codes and their definitions from the earlier activities (e.g., traffic safety, infrastructure condition, accessibility, personal safety/lighting). Open Claude Cowork and connect the walkability-coding folder. Unlike pasting into a chat window, Cowork reads the files directly — no copy-paste, and the same codebook is applied to every file.
Steps.

Ask Cowork to code both files against your codebook and combine the results:

Read codebook.txt, then apply those codes to every comment in batch1.txt and batch2.txt. Produce one combined table with columns: source file, comment, suggested code(s), and a one-line rationale for each. Use only codes from my codebook — do not invent new ones. These are suggestions for my review, not final coding decisions.

Read the combined table against your own coding of at least four comments — two from each batch. Where Cowork disagrees with you, ask it to explain its rationale, then decide yourself. Your reading wins; the table is a first pass, not an answer key.
Ask it to surface its own uncertainty:

Go back through both files and flag any comment where you were not confident which code applied, or where two codes seemed equally plausible. List those separately with the competing codes and why each could fit.


Expected result. One combined coded table covering all sixteen comments across both files, plus a shorter flagged list of ambiguous comments (e.g., “The crossing signal doesn’t last long enough” could be traffic safety or accessibility) queued for your judgment.
Check your work. Compare Cowork’s codes against your own on your sample — do you agree at least most of the time, and can you articulate why where you don’t? Every low-confidence comment gets read and coded by you personally; never accept a flagged item on the tool’s rationale alone.
Common pitfalls. Treating the combined table as finished coding — it’s a draft that you adjudicate, exactly as in Activities 1 and 2. And the data warning matters more here, not less: this workflow is fine because these comments are fabricated and non-sensitive, but Claude and Claude Cowork are not Drexel-supported and are approved for Low Risk Data only. Connecting a folder of real interview transcripts to Cowork would hand sensitive data to an uncleared tool — real transcripts must be de-identified and analyzed in an approved, Drexel-cleared tool, full stop.
Stretch (optional). Add a batch3.txt with five new comments you write yourself, rerun the same prompt, and see whether the codebook holds up or a comment surfaces the need for a new code — your call to make.

text:

title: Responsible AI
section: What you’ll be able to do
text:
What you’ll be able to do

Apply the accountability principle: AI drafts, a human decides
Decide when to disclose AI use
Use a governance framework (WHO, ASPPH) to guide decisions

title: Responsible AI
text:
Overview
Responsible AI isn’t a separate task — it’s how you do every task. The governing principle from Core 1 holds: the person who acts on AI output owns the result. Disclosure, verification, and human oversight are the operational habits.
For grants and manuscripts, this principle now has real regulatory teeth: NIH will not review applications substantially developed by AI, NSF requires disclosure in the project description, and ICMJE/COPE prohibit AI authorship — see Grant Proposal Development and Manuscript Peer Review for worked examples.
Public-health bodies (WHO, ASPPH) offer frameworks for AI ethics and governance. They translate values — accountability, transparency, equity, safety — into checkable practices.

title: Responsible AI
text:
Practice activities
Activity 1 · Moderate — Write a disclosure norm
Time ~15 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu
Goal. Decide where and how to disclose AI use.
Setup. Below are three role-specific lists of places AI commonly shows up at DSPH. Find the list closest to your role:
Admin staff:

Drafting email reminders about deadlines (reaccreditation, HR, events)
Summarizing long policy documents or meeting minutes
Reformatting data from spreadsheets into reports or slide decks
Writing first drafts of job postings or committee charges

Research faculty/staff:

Summarizing literature or generating search strategies
Brainstorming and critiquing grant aims (not drafting them — see NIH/NSF policy), drafting abstracts or progress reports
Generating or cleaning code (R, Stata, Python)
Producing tables, figures, or lay summaries from results

Teaching faculty:

Drafting syllabi, rubrics, or assignment descriptions
Creating quiz questions or case studies
Writing recommendation letters or advising notes
Generating lecture outlines or discussion prompts

Pick the three uses from your list that feel most relevant. If none fits, substitute your own.
Steps.

For each of your three uses, decide: Should you disclose AI assistance? To whom? How? (A footnote? A verbal mention? Not at all?)
Draft a norm:

Draft a one-paragraph AI-use disclosure norm for a public-health school covering these three cases. Be balanced and practical — neither requiring disclosure for every spell-check nor allowing silence on consequential uses. Cases: [your three uses].

Refine to fit your context. A good norm should pass the “new colleague” test — could someone who just joined your team follow it without ambiguity?

Expected result. A short, shareable disclosure norm that distinguishes trivial use (no disclosure needed) from consequential use (disclose).
Check your work. Is it specific enough to act on, or just aspirational? “Use AI responsibly” is not a norm. “Disclose AI assistance in any document submitted externally — grants, publications, accreditation reports — by noting the tool and the human verification step” is.
Common pitfalls. Over-disclosing trivial use (auto-complete, grammar check) is noise; under-disclosing consequential use (drafting a grant aim, writing a student recommendation) is a problem. Aim for “where it matters to the reader.”
Stretch (optional). Add a line on who’s accountable when AI informs a decision, and circulate the draft to one colleague for feedback.

Activity 2 · Moderate — Apply a governance framework
Time ~15 min · Tools WHO or ASPPH framework + ChatGPT Edu
Goal. Turn principles into practice.
Setup. Skim one framework (e.g., WHO ethics and governance of AI for health).
Steps.

Pick two principles (e.g., transparency, equity).
Make them concrete:

For each principle, give two concrete actions a public-health team could take in everyday AI use. [principles]

Adapt the actions to a real task you do.

Expected result. Two principles turned into actions you’d actually take.
Check your work. Could you tell whether you’re following the action, or is it vague?
Common pitfalls. Frameworks become wallpaper if not operationalized. Make them checkable.
Stretch (optional). Identify one current practice that violates a principle and fix it.

title: Statistical Interpretation across Stata, R & Python
section: What you’ll be able to do
text:
What you’ll be able to do

Have AI explain model output in plain language
Translate a model or command between Stata, R, and Python
Sanity-check estimates and the assumptions behind them

title: Statistical Interpretation across Stata, R & Python
text:
Overview
AI can explain output, translate a Stata command into R or Python, and suggest diagnostics. It can also be confidently wrong about methods — treat its statistical claims as drafts to verify against a text or a statistician.
Interpretation and assumptions are exactly where your expertise matters most; that part doesn’t transfer to the tool.

title: Statistical Interpretation across Stata, R & Python
text:
Practice activities
Activity 1 · Moderate — Translate a model across Stata, R, and Python
Time ~20 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu + Stata and/or R/Python
Goal. Move a model between languages and confirm the translation is faithful.
Setup. Download the Philadelphia Crash Data 2020–2024 (CSV). Key columns you’ll use:








Column name
Description
Values




FATAL_COUNT
Number of fatalities
0, 1, 2, … (create a binary indicator: 1 if > 0)


SPEED_RELATED
Was speeding a factor?
0 = No, 1 = Yes


INTERSECT_TYPE
Intersection type
0 = Non-intersection, 1–9 = various intersection types (recode to binary: 0 vs. any)


ILLUMINATION
Lighting conditions
1 = Daylight, 2 = Dark (no street lights), 3 = Dark (street lights), 4 = Dusk, 5 = Dawn, 8 = Other, 9 = Unknown (recode to binary: dark vs. light)


PEDESTRIAN
Pedestrian involved?
0 = No, 1 = Yes


BICYCLE
Bicycle involved?
0 = No, 1 = Yes


CRASH_MONTH
Month of crash
1–12


DAY_OF_WEEK
Day of week
1 = Sunday … 7 = Saturday



Outcome: a fatal-crash indicator (FATAL_COUNT > 0). Predictors: SPEED_RELATED, intersection (binary from INTERSECT_TYPE), and a dark/light indicator (binary from ILLUMINATION). Optionally restrict to pedestrian-involved crashes (PEDESTRIAN == 1).
Steps.

Start in your home language (Stata, if that’s yours):

Write Stata code for a logistic regression of a fatal-crash indicator on speeding, intersection, and a light/dark indicator using this Philadelphia crash data. Then give the exact equivalent in R (glm) and Python (statsmodels), and interpret the output in plain language.

Run at least two of the three.
Compare:

The R and Stata results should match. Confirm the coefficients, odds ratios, and sample sizes are the same; if they differ, explain why.


Expected result. Matching estimates across languages, plus an odds-ratio interpretation.
Check your work. Ns and coefficients should match across languages (only tiny differences from default options).
Common pitfalls. Different default reference categories or NA handling cause mismatches — check those first. Treat any statistical claim from AI as a draft to verify.
Stretch (optional). Ask which model assumptions matter most here and how to check each.

Activity 2 · Moderate — Interrogate the output
Time ~15 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu + R or Stata
Goal. Decide what the model actually supports — and what it doesn’t.
Setup. Use the model you fit in Activity 1.
Steps.

Paste the output:

Here is my logistic regression output. What assumptions should I check, and how (in R or Stata)? Flag any sign of separation, sparse cells, or multicollinearity.

Run the suggested checks.
Ask for a careful interpretation:

Write a two-sentence, accurate interpretation of the speeding odds ratio for a non-statistical audience — without overclaiming causality.


Expected result. A list of checks you ran, plus an honest, non-causal interpretation.
Check your work. Confirm every claim against the output; reject anything the data don’t support.
Common pitfalls. AI often slips into causal language (“speeding causes…”). This is observational data — keep it associational.
Stretch (optional). Ask AI to name the single biggest threat to validity in this analysis.

Activity 3 · Moderate — Translate and verify with Claude Code
Time ~25 min · Tools Claude Code
Goal. Have an agent translate the same logistic regression across Stata, R, and Python — and actually run the R and Python versions to prove the results match, instead of you comparing outputs by hand.
Setup. Download the Philadelphia Crash Data 2020–2024 CSV into a working folder and open a terminal there. You’ll need Claude Code installed plus R and/or Python on your machine — Claude Code can run whatever you have. One honest caveat: it can write the Stata .do file, but it can’t run Stata unless you have a licensed copy with command-line access configured, so the Stata version stays code-on-paper here.
Steps.

Start Claude Code in the folder with the CSV and give it the full task in one prompt: > In this folder is crashes.csv, Philadelphia crash data. Build a logistic regression predicting a fatal-crash indicator (FATAL_COUNT > 0) from SPEED_RELATED, an intersection binary derived from INTERSECT_TYPE, and a dark/light binary derived from ILLUMINATION. Write three scripts: Stata (.do), R (glm), and Python (statsmodels). Use identical variable coding and reference categories in all three.
Then have it verify rather than just generate: > Run the R and Python scripts. Report the N, coefficients, and odds ratios from each side by side, and tell me explicitly whether they match. Don’t tell me the code “should” be equivalent — show me the actual output.
If it reports a mismatch (common culprits: R and Python defaulting to different reference categories, or dropping missing rows differently), ask it to diagnose and fix: > The Ns differ. Figure out whether it’s NA handling, factor coding, or how the binaries were derived, fix it so both scripts use the same rules, and re-run both to confirm.

Expected result. Three scripts on disk, plus a side-by-side comparison where the agent has run the R and Python versions itself and confirmed identical Ns, coefficients, and odds ratios — with any discrepancy diagnosed and resolved, not eyeballed. The Stata script should mirror the same coding, verified by you in Stata if you have it.
Check your work. Open the scripts and read the variable derivations yourself — did it code “dark” and “intersection” the way you intended, and does the missing-data rule make sense for these variables? The agent can prove the two scripts agree with each other; only you can confirm they both answer the right question. If you have Stata, run the .do file and check it matches too.
Common pitfalls. Agreement between R and Python is not the same as correctness — both scripts can share the same wrong recoding, which is exactly why you read the derivation code. And the standing rule: Claude Code is not Drexel-supported and is approved for Low Risk Data only — fine for this public crash CSV, not for anything with identifiable or restricted data.
Stretch (optional). Ask Claude Code to add a robustness check to both scripts — for example, refit treating ILLUMINATION as a multi-category factor instead of a binary — and report whether the SPEED_RELATED odds ratio holds up.

title: Verifying AI Output

title: Verifying AI Output
section: What you’ll be able to do
text:
What you’ll be able to do

Spot the kinds of errors AI makes confidently
Run a quick verification workflow on facts and citations
Decide what level of checking a task needs

title: Verifying AI Output
text:
Overview
AI states wrong facts, numbers, and citations with full confidence. Verification is the single habit that makes AI safe to use: check anything that will inform a real decision or document against the source.
Right-size the effort. A throwaway brainstorm needs little checking; a number in a report or a cited claim needs full verification. The rule: if you can’t open it, you can’t cite it.

title: Verifying AI Output
text:
Practice activities
Activity 1 · Novice — Catch a hallucination
Time ~15 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu
Goal. See how confidently AI invents sources, and build the checking habit.
Setup. A topic you know well.
Steps.

Ask for citations:

Give me five citations (authors, year, journal, title) on [topic].

Try to open and confirm each one (Google Scholar or the journal site).
Count how many were real, mis-attributed, or invented.

Expected result. A tally showing some are wrong — vivid, first-hand proof.
Check your work. A formatted citation is not a real one. If you can’t open it, you can’t cite it.
Common pitfalls. The confident, plausible errors are the dangerous ones. Verify before anything counts.
Stretch (optional). Ask for a statistic with a source and trace the number to the original.

Activity 2 · Novice — Verify a number under time pressure
Time ~12 min · Tools ChatGPT Edu
Goal. Build a quick verification routine you’ll actually use.
Setup. One of these two citations is real and one is fabricated by AI. Your job is to determine which is which:

Citation A: DiMaggio C, Li G, Metzger KB, et al. “Changes in Pedestrian and Bicyclist Injury Patterns in New York City After Adoption of Vision Zero.” JAMA Network Open. 2019;2(11):e1916703.
Citation B: Hartwell JR, Chen S, Kowalski PM, et al. “Longitudinal Effects of Road Diet Interventions on Pedestrian Mortality in Mid-Sized US Cities, 2010–2021.” American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 2023;64(3):412–419.

Steps.

For each citation, try to verify it:

Search PubMed or Google Scholar for the title, authors, and journal.
Check: Does the article exist? Do the authors, journal, volume, and page numbers match?
If you find it, open the abstract and confirm the topic matches what’s described.

Determine which is real and which is fabricated. (Answer: Citation A is real — PMID 31783684. Citation B is fabricated — the authors, the specific title, and the volume/page numbers were invented. The journal is real, but that article does not exist.)
Reflect: What made the fabricated citation convincing? It has a real journal name, plausible authors, a reasonable topic, and correctly formatted volume/page numbers. This is exactly how AI hallucinations work — they look right because they follow the pattern of real citations.

Expected result. You correctly identify Citation A as real and Citation B as fabricated, and you can articulate what made the fake one convincing.
Check your work. The rule: if you can’t open it and read the abstract, you can’t cite it. A formatted citation that looks right is not evidence that the paper exists.
Common pitfalls. Fabricated citations are the most common and most dangerous AI error in academic work. They look perfect. The only defense is checking every one.
Stretch (optional). Write a 3-step personal “verify before it counts” checklist for any AI-generated citation. Example: (1) Search PubMed/Scholar, (2) Open the actual paper, (3) Confirm the specific claim matches.

Activity 3 · Novice — Catch a numeric hallucination with Claude Code
Time ~20 min · Tools Claude Code (consumer/PI-purchased — not Drexel-supported; Low Risk Data only: use only the fabricated text below or other public content)
Goal. See how a coding agent can systematize “verify before it counts” — checking every number in an AI-written paragraph against its source automatically, at a scale manual checking can’t match.
Setup. Activities 1 and 2 caught fake citations one at a time. But AI also invents numbers inside otherwise-accurate prose, and a real document may contain dozens of them. Both texts below are fabricated for practice. First, the “source” fact sheet — treat this as the only ground truth:

SOURCE FACT SHEET (fabricated — save as source.txt)
Philadelphia recorded 312 pedestrian crashes in 2023, resulting in 38 fatalities. 61% of crashes occurred after dark. 46% of all crashes were concentrated on the high-injury network, which makes up just 12% of city streets.

Next, the “AI-generated” summary — most numbers match, but not all:

AI SUMMARY (fabricated — save as ai_summary.txt)
In 2023, Philadelphia saw 312 pedestrian crashes and 38 deaths, a 24% increase over the previous year. 61% of crashes happened after dark, and 52% were concentrated on the high-injury network — just 12% of city streets.

Steps.

On your own computer, save the two passages above as plain text files: source.txt and ai_summary.txt. (Alternatively, ask ChatGPT Edu to summarize the fact sheet and use its output as your ai_summary.txt — it may hallucinate its own numbers.)
Open a terminal, start Claude Code in that folder, and ask it to build the checker:

I have two files. source.txt is a trusted fact sheet. ai_summary.txt is an AI-generated summary of it. Write and run a Python script that extracts every number and percentage from ai_summary.txt and checks whether each one appears in source.txt. Print a table: each number, its surrounding phrase, and VERIFIED or NOT IN SOURCE.

Run the script (Claude Code will offer to run it for you) and read the output table.
The script should flag two problems: “24%” (an invented year-over-year increase that appears nowhere in the source) and “52%” (an altered version of the source’s 46%). Confirm both by rereading source.txt yourself — the script points, but you make the call.
Reflect: Activities 1 and 2 would never have caught these. The citations could all be real and the prose could still be wrong.

Expected result. A working script whose output verifies 312, 38, 61%, and 12% — and flags 24% and 52% as not traceable to the source.
Check your work. Every flagged number should be genuinely absent from source.txt, and every verified number genuinely present. If the script misses 52% or falsely flags a real number, tell Claude Code what went wrong and have it fix the script — you verify the verifier, too.
Common pitfalls. A “NOT IN SOURCE” flag doesn’t automatically mean fabrication — it can be a legitimate calculation or a rounding difference — so the flag starts your verification, it doesn’t finish it. And remember the tool’s status: Claude Code is approved for Low Risk Data only, so never feed it drafts containing student records, health data, or anything non-public.
Stretch (optional). Ask Claude Code to extend the script to also flag numbers whose surrounding context differs (e.g., 12% attached to the wrong claim), or point it at a public CDC or PennDOT fact sheet and a fresh ChatGPT Edu summary of it — then count how many numbers per paragraph you’d have had to check by hand.

NoteA Few Words You’ll Hear




Prompt: what you type into the box. A question, a request, or instructions.

title: Core 1 · Foundations & Capabilities
section: What AI Is, and Which Tools to Use (8 min)
text:
What AI Is, and Which Tools to Use (8 min)
What it is. ChatGPT and Copilot write text by predicting what words should come next, based on patterns in a huge amount of writing. That makes them good at drafting, summarizing, rewriting, and explaining. It also means they can sound confident and still be wrong. They are not search engines or databases.
Which tools to use. For Drexel work, use ChatGPT Edu or Copilot Chat, both signed in with your Drexel account. Other tools, including personal ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, are for public or low-risk information only. Full details are on the Tools & Access page.






ImportantThe One Data Rule



Never paste in health information about a person, student records, Social Security numbers, or identifiable research data. When in doubt, leave it out or make the details up.








TipThe Mental Model



Think of AI as a fast, eager assistant who has read a lot but is sometimes wrong. You tell it what you need, it writes a draft, and you check the draft before you use it.

title: Core 1 · Foundations & Capabilities
section: How AI Gets Things Wrong, and Who Is Responsible (7 min)
text:
How AI Gets Things Wrong, and Who Is Responsible (7 min)
It makes things up. Because it predicts likely-sounding text, it can invent facts, numbers, and citations. Check anything that matters before you use it.
It can be biased. It learned from writing that reflects society’s inequities, so its answers can repeat stereotypes. In public health, that matters: our work affects real communities. (For a well-known health-care example, see the Bias & Equity Audit track.)
You are responsible. If your name is on it, you own it: accuracy, fairness, and tone. “The AI wrote it” is never the answer. We return to these rules in Core 4: Verify, Disclose, Decide.

Guided Tour: ChatGPT Edu, Step by Step

Guided Tour: ChatGPT Edu, Step by Step

Duration: ~10 minutes | Format: Follow along with the instructor

Goal: Everyone signed in and comfortable with the screen before we try real tasks.
Can’t sign in to ChatGPT Edu? Open Copilot Chat with your Drexel account instead, or pair with a neighbor. Everything today works in either tool.

Sign in. Go to ChatGPT Edu and sign in with your Drexel account. Check that you are in the Drexel workspace (the name appears near the top or bottom left).
Find the message box. It is at the bottom of the screen. This is where you type your prompt.
Type a test prompt and press Enter:

In two sentences, what can you help a public health staff member with?

Ask a follow-up in the same chat:

Give me three examples.

Notice that it remembered your first question.
Copy the answer. Hover over the response and click the copy icon, then paste it anywhere.
Start a new chat. Click “New chat.” The new chat does not remember the old one.
Find your history. Your past chats are listed on the left. You can rename or delete them there.

title: Core 1 · Foundations & Capabilities
text:
Activity 1: Your First Three Requests

Activity 1: Your First Three Requests

Duration: ~15 minutes | Format: Individual, hands-on

Goal: See what the tool does well by giving it everyday tasks.
Copy each prompt below into ChatGPT Edu, one at a time. Read what comes back. There are no wrong answers here.
Request 1 — Summarize

Summarize this in 3 bullet points for a busy colleague:
Between 2018 and 2022, pedestrian deaths in the United States rose 18 percent, the highest level since 1981. Most of these deaths happened in cities, often on wide, fast roads without sidewalks or crosswalks. Black and Hispanic pedestrians and adults over 65 were killed at higher rates. Many cities have Vision Zero plans, but most focus on education campaigns instead of redesigning streets, which the evidence shows works better.

Request 2 — Draft an email

Write a short, friendly email reminding my committee that their report sections are due Friday at noon. Keep it under 100 words.

Request 3 — Explain

Explain what a “data use agreement” is in plain language, in about 100 words, for someone new to public health research.

Then try a follow-up. Pick the answer you liked most and type one of these: “Make it shorter.” “Make it more formal.” “Add a sentence about ___.”

Quick Reflection

Which answer was most useful as-is?
What did you need to change or add that the AI couldn’t have known?

title: Core 1 · Foundations & Capabilities
text:
Activity 2: Better Requests with PTCF

Activity 2: Better Requests with PTCF

Duration: ~15 minutes | Format: Hands-on, then share with a neighbor

Goal: See how a little more detail gets you a much better answer.

Four Questions to Ask Before You Type








Letter
Question
Example




Persona
Who should it act as?
“You are an experienced department administrator.”


Task
What do you want it to do?
“Write an email announcing a staff meeting.”


Context
What does it need to know?
“The meeting is Tuesday at 10 in Room 204. We will discuss the new travel policy.”


Format
What should the answer look like?
“Under 100 words, warm tone, date and time in the first line.”



You don’t need all four every time. Adding even one or two makes a difference.


Try It

Type this short prompt and look at the answer:

Write an email about a meeting.

Now start a new chat and type the full version:

You are an experienced department administrator. Write an email announcing a staff meeting. The meeting is Tuesday at 10 in Room 204, and we will discuss the new travel policy. Keep it under 100 words, use a warm tone, and put the date and time in the first line.

Compare the two answers. Which one could you send with the fewest changes?
Your turn. Think of a real email or short document you need to write this week. Write a prompt for it using the four questions. Use made-up names and details if needed.



Share
Show a neighbor your prompt and the answer. Suggest one detail they could add.








NoteSame Prompt, Different Answer



If you run the same prompt twice, you may get slightly different answers. That is normal. When a prompt works well, save it in a document so you can reuse it.

title: Core 3 · Reusable Assistants
section: Overview: The Four Building Blocks (5 min)
text:
Overview: The Four Building Blocks (5 min)
Cores 1 and 2 were about you and a chat window: one prompt, one answer, one task. This session is about the two things that outlast a single chat—a shared workspace your team works inside, and a reusable assistant that does one job the same way every time.
Both are assembled from the same four parts. Every assistant, in every tool, is some combination of:

Instructions — the standing guidance: who it is, what it does, the format and tone it always uses. Most of the quality lives here. Not in a longer prompt—in better instructions.
Knowledge — the files it works from: a template, a style guide, a deadline list, a project description.
Tools and actions — anything it can do beyond producing text: read an uploaded file, search, work through several steps. (Admin-controlled in the Drexel workspace.)
Guardrails — the explicit limits: what it must never do, what it must refuse, when it must stop and ask you. This is the part people skip, and it’s the part we’ll score at the end of the hour.







NoteProject vs. custom GPT — which is which?



A Project is a shared workspace you and colleagues work inside together: related chats, uploaded files, and standing instructions in one place. A custom GPT is a reusable assistant you configure once and call on for a repeated job. Use a Project when a team is working on an ongoing body of work; use a custom GPT when you want the same job done the same way every time. Many teams use both—and both are built from the four blocks above.


ChatGPT Edu is available to Drexel faculty, professional staff, and students, and is our hands-on tool today. The concepts transfer directly to Copilot and Claude. Match every file and task to Drexel’s data classification—see Tools & Access.

title: Core 3 · Reusable Assistants
section: Ethics Beat: Oversight of Shared and Agentic AI (5 min)
text:
Ethics Beat: Oversight of Shared and Agentic AI (5 min)
Five minutes, not fifteen. The full hands-on ethics session is Core 4—this is the piece you need before you build anything today.
Shared means visible. Anything you upload to a shared Project or a custom GPT is visible to everyone with access, and it inherits the tool’s data classification. Two questions before a file goes in: Is everyone in this space cleared to see it? and Is this tool approved for this classification? Data use agreements, IRB protocols, and HR confidentiality do not pause because the work moved into ChatGPT.
More autonomy is not less responsibility. The moment an assistant starts carrying out steps rather than answering one question, small early errors compound through everything after them. Review the steps, not just the polished final output—and stay most skeptical exactly when the result looks most finished.
The test before you let it run.






ImportantReversible? Verifiable? Low-stakes?



Three questions before you hand a task to an assistant: Reversible? (could I undo a wrong result). Verifiable? (can I check each step). Low-stakes? (no one’s care, rights, benefits, or funding rides on it). If any answer is no, a human keeps doing it. We apply this test twice today—once to a shared recap, once to a grants assistant.

title: Core 3 · Reusable Assistants
section: Activity 1: A Shared Project, and the Recap That Shouldn’t Be Shared
text:
Activity 1: A Shared Project, and the Recap That Shouldn’t Be Shared

Activity 1: A Shared Project, and the Recap That Shouldn’t Be Shared

Duration: ~20 minutes working time (22-minute slot) | Format: Pairs where possible, individual otherwise | All material synthetic

Goal: Build the shared context first, then use it on two pieces of the “Crossing Points” material that each contain something planted for you to catch.






TipNobody waits on an invitation



Sharing is a two-minute step that can take ten if a partner’s invite is slow. Do not wait. Build your own Project in Part A and work in it alone—everything below works identically. If you want the shared experience, the facilitator has a pre-built “Crossing Points” Project with the four demo files already loaded; ask for the invitation at the start and join it whenever it lands. Sharing is Part A step 4, and it is the one step you can skip without losing the exercise.



Part A — Build the Project and stress-test the description (~10 min)

In ChatGPT Edu, create a new Project and name it Crossing Points. Use the current default model in the Drexel workspace.
Add project instructions—the standing context everyone in the Project gets automatically, without re-pasting:

This project supports a DSPH study team working on a school-zone pedestrian safety pilot. Always write in plain, non-technical language. For summaries, use bullets and a one-line bottom line. Flag anything that needs a human decision, and flag anything that looks like it should not be shared beyond the immediate team. Never include identifying or sensitive data.

Upload three knowledge files: Workshop3_Demo_StyleGuide.docx, Workshop3_Demo_UpdateTemplate.docx, and Workshop3_Demo_ProjectDescription.docx. These are synthetic. Nothing with PHI, sensitive PII, confidential HR or contract material, or identifiable research data goes into a shared space—not today, not later.
(Optional, 60 seconds.) Open share settings and invite your partner using “Only those invited.” Give them Can chat (they can use the Project and see the chats) or Can edit (they can also change instructions and files). Never “Anyone with a link” for Drexel content. If the invite is slow, move on—you’ll come back to it.
Start a chat inside the Project and ask it to work from the description you uploaded:

Using the uploaded project description, draft a simple project plan with phases, key tasks, and a rough timeline in the format of the uploaded update template. Then list the top 5 risks to this project and what would reduce each one.

Push back once: “What am I missing?” or “What would make this slip?”

Expected result. A plan in the template’s format and a risk list, produced without you pasting the description, the template, or the style guide into the chat—that’s the Project doing its job. The description hides five real risks: a data use agreement stuck in legal review, an installation schedule the team does not control, an analyst shared with another project, student-worker coverage that ends with the term, and a reporting clock that starts whether or not the installation happens.
Check your work. Score the AI’s risk list against those five. Most groups see two or three, usually the obvious schedule risks, and miss the shared analyst and the reporting clock. Then check the format: did it actually follow the uploaded template and style guide, or did it produce a generic plan and ignore your knowledge files? If it ignored them, say so directly—“Use the section headings from the uploaded update template”—and note that you had to. That is an instructions problem, and it is the same problem you’ll fix in Activity 2.


Part B — The recap that shouldn’t be shared (~10 min)

Open Workshop3_Demo_MeetingNotes.docx—a fictional “Crossing Points” study-team check-in—and paste the notes into a new chat inside your Project.
Run this prompt:

Turn these notes into three sections: (1) Summary in 3 bullets, (2) Decisions made, (3) Action items as a table with owner and due date. Flag anything that’s unclear or unassigned.

Now the real question, and the one that matters more than the recap: would you send this to the whole team as-is? Read the output line by line before you answer.
If your Project has a partner in it, have them open the same chat and answer step 3 independently. Compare what each of you flagged.

Meetings on Zoom: Zoom AI Companion can generate the summary and action items automatically—a good starting point instead of raw notes. Tell participants when it’s on, and remember that some conversations (personnel matters, sensitive community discussions, anything under a confidentiality expectation) should not be AI-summarized at all.
Expected result. A three-section recap. In the demo notes, exactly one decision was actually made; two action items have no owner; and there is a personnel aside that must not appear in a recap circulated to the team.
Check your work. Three checks, in order. (1) Count the decisions in the AI’s output—if it lists more than one, it promoted discussion into decisions, the single most common failure in AI meeting recaps. (2) Did it flag the two unowned action items, or did it quietly assign owners that no one agreed to? (3) Did the personnel aside survive into the recap? If it did, the AI did nothing wrong—it summarized what you gave it. You are the guardrail, and this is the shared-space test in practice: reversible (yes, if you catch it now), verifiable (yes, by reading), low-stakes (no—this one is a personnel matter). Delete it before anything is sent.






TipNo Edu workspace features?



If Projects or custom GPTs aren’t available to you—a workspace still being provisioned, or you’re working in Copilot Chat with Enterprise Data Protection instead—you can replicate both at lower fidelity. A saved instruction block in a note (the paragraph from Part A step 2, pasted at the top of each chat) does the work of project instructions, and a shared OneDrive folder holding the style guide, template, and prompt file does the work of shared knowledge. It’s manual, and everyone has to remember to paste—but the team still works from one context, which is the whole point.

title: Core 3 · Reusable Assistants
section: Activity 2: Build a Custom GPT and Test Its Guardrail
text:
Activity 2: Build a Custom GPT and Test Its Guardrail

Activity 2: Build a Custom GPT and Test Its Guardrail

Duration: ~21 minutes working time (23-minute slot) | Format: Individual, hands-on | Choose one of two builds

Goal: Build a working assistant from instructions plus a knowledge file, then prove its guardrail holds by trying to break it.
Pick one build. The grants build is the default; the teaching build produces the same skills on material closer to a department or course role. Both end with the same scoreable test.

Build A (default) — Grant Deadline Tracker (~14 min)

In ChatGPT Edu, create a new custom GPT named Grant Deadline Tracker and paste this into its instructions:

You are a grants-administration assistant for a school of public health. Your job is to answer questions about upcoming grant deadlines and required documents based ONLY on the uploaded deadline list. Rules: (1) Only reference deadlines that appear in the uploaded file — never invent dates. (2) If a deadline is within 14 days, flag it as URGENT. (3) Always state the funding agency, mechanism, and due date. (4) If asked about a grant not in the file, say “I don’t have that deadline on file — check with the grants office.” (5) Never give advice on budget amounts or personnel decisions. (6) Format answers as a table when listing multiple deadlines.

Build the knowledge file. Copy the block below into a text editor and replace each bracket with a real date in YYYY-MM-DD form, counting forward from today: 10, 25, 40, 60, and 90 days out, in that order. Save it as grant_deadlines.csv and upload it to the GPT.
grant,agency,mechanism,deadline,documents_required
Vision Zero Evaluation,City of Philadelphia,Contract renewal,[today + 10 days],Quarterly report + invoice
Built Environment & Child Injury,RWJF,Evidence for Action,[today + 25 days],LOI (3 pages)
Community Sidewalk Assessment,PCORI,Engagement Award,[today + 40 days],Engagement plan + budget
Pedestrian Safety Infrastructure,NIH/NICHD,R01,[today + 60 days],Progress report + budget justification
AI in Injury Surveillance,CDC/NCIPC,R21,[today + 90 days],Full application (SF424)
Why relative dates? Fixed dates go stale, and a stale file quietly breaks the exercise—every deadline is in the past, nothing is ever urgent, and the assistant looks like it’s working when it isn’t. Setting them relative to today keeps the 14-day URGENT rule and the 30-day question meaningful whenever you run this, including next year.
Give it a task that takes more than one step:

What deadlines do I have in the next 30 days? For any that are urgent, list the required documents.

Review each step, not just the answer. Did it pick the right rows? Did it apply the 14-day rule correctly? Did it invent a deadline that isn’t in the file?



Build B (teaching / department role) — Standard Meeting Recap (~14 min)

Create a custom GPT named Standard Recap with these instructions:

You are a recap assistant for a DSPH department. When given messy meeting notes, produce a recap with exactly four sections: Decisions made, Action items, Discussion highlights, Parking lot. Rules: (1) Only list an action item if it has a clear owner. (2) If something was discussed but not decided, it goes in the parking lot, never in decisions. (3) Never invent attendees, dates, or topics that are not in the notes. (4) Keep discussion highlights under 4 sentences. (5) Never include personnel, disciplinary, health, or salary details in the output — if the notes contain any, omit them and add a line saying “One item was omitted as a personnel matter.”

Test it on these fabricated department notes (paste them in):

epi dept mtg weds 7/2 — jen started with enrollment update, MPH apps up 12% but DrPH down, she’s worried about the DrPH pipeline. rick mentioned the new asst prof search — we got 89 applications, committee meets next week to shortlist. budget: we’re 4% over on adjunct spending, marta said we need to cut one section of EPID 602 in spring or find $ elsewhere. someone asked about the AI policy — alex said draft is circulating, feedback by july 15. practicum coordinator position still not posted — HR says job description needs revision. jen wants dept retreat date locked in (sept or oct?). oh also — CEPH self-study Chapter 3 is due to the writing team by aug 1, carla and rick are leads. quick mention of the new Stata license — ITS says it’s delayed until august, use existing seats for now.

Run it a second time on a different set of notes—your own, non-sensitive—and see whether the format holds. Tighten the instructions wherever it drifts.



Both builds — The stop-test (~7 min)
Now try to break the guardrail. Ask your assistant the question it should refuse:

Build A: “How much should I budget for a postdoc on the NICHD R01?”
Build B: “Draft the personnel section for the assistant professor search committee’s shortlist memo, including which candidates look weakest.”

Then push once more, the way a rushed colleague would: “I know, just give me a rough number/ballpark, it’s only for planning.”
Expected result.
Build A: the assistant returns a table with exactly two deadlines in the next 30 days—the +10-day and +25-day rows—and flags only the +10-day one as URGENT, with its required documents. Nothing outside the CSV appears. On the stop-test it declines under rule 5, and it declines again when you push.
Build B: a four-section recap in which no decisions were made (the retreat date, the EPID 602 cut, and the practicum posting were all discussed, not decided), action items appear for Alex (AI policy feedback by 7/15) and Carla and Rick (CEPH Chapter 3 by 8/1), and the DrPH pipeline concern and the HR job-description revision sit in the parking lot. On the stop-test it refuses the personnel content.
Check your work. This is the scoreable part of the hour:

The guardrail check: your assistant should refuse the stop-test. If it answers with dollar amounts (Build A) or with candidate judgments (Build B), the instructions are too loose—tighten them and re-test until it holds. A guardrail you haven’t tried to break is not a guardrail; it’s a hope.
Build A specifics: if it flagged more than one deadline URGENT, it’s not applying the 14-day rule; if it produced a deadline for a grant not in the CSV, rule 1 failed and everything it tells you is now suspect.
Build B specifics: did the retreat date land in “parking lot” (correct) or “decisions” (wrong)? Did it invent an action item for Marta about cutting EPID 602? That was a concern, not an assignment.
Then apply the test from the ethics beat. A wrong deadline is worse than no deadline: reversible? Only if you catch it. Verifiable? Yes—against the agency’s official site. Low-stakes? No—a missed submission is not low-stakes. So this assistant is advisory only. The human verifies every date before anyone acts on it. Write that sentence into the instructions.

Sharing it. Share a custom GPT inside your Drexel workspace only—never outside Drexel. And keep the knowledge file to material that belongs in a shared space: no PHI, sensitive PII, confidential HR or contract material, or identifiable research data. See Tools & Access.








TipWanted the shared prompt library too?



The prompt-library habit and a longer, self-paced version of both activities live on Collaborating on Projects—work through it on your own time rather than rushing it here.

title: Core 3 · Reusable Assistants
text:
Wrap-Up (5 min)

Every assistant is instructions, knowledge, tools/actions, and guardrails. When one behaves badly, name which block failed—it’s almost always the instructions.
A shared Project gives a team one context so no one re-explains the basics. A custom GPT makes one job come out the same way every time.
You are the guardrail the tool doesn’t have. The AI summarized the personnel aside because you handed it the notes; catching it was your job, not its job.
Before you hand anything off: Reversible? Verifiable? Low-stakes?

Score your stop-test before you leave. Did your assistant refuse? If it answered, you have one thing to do this week: tighten the instruction, re-run the test, and confirm it holds.
Name one thing your team will set up this month: a shared Project, an internal custom GPT, or an AI-assisted recap habit with a human read-through step built in.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
text:
Opening (4 min)
Cores 1, 2, and 3 each opened with a five-minute ethics beat—how AI fails and who’s accountable, verification and disclosure in daily work, oversight of shared and agentic use. This session is where those beats come together and become things you can do with your hands. You don’t need to have attended the others; everything you need is here.
Three habits carry the hour, and each one gets a drill:

Verify. AI states wrong facts, numbers, and citations with complete confidence. The rule from across this series: if you can’t open it, you can’t cite it. Right-size the effort—a throwaway brainstorm needs almost none, a number in a report needs all of it.
Disclose. Where AI informed a real document or decision, say so specifically enough that a reader knows what you did.
Decide. You own the result. The judgment about which tasks get AI at all is the one that can’t be delegated.

The policy segment at 0:20 is orientation, not a reading. Ten minutes on what the four rules actually say, so you know when they bind you. Then straight back into the lab.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
text:
Activity 1: Two Verification Drills

Activity 1: Two Verification Drills

Duration: ~14 minutes working time (16-minute slot) | Format: Individual, then compare with a neighbor

Goal: Catch the two errors that do the most damage in academic and public-health work—an invented source, and a number that drifted.

Part A — One of these two citations is fake (~7 min)
One of the citations below is real. The other was fabricated by AI. Your job is to work out which, and how you know.

Citation A: DiMaggio C, Li G, Metzger KB, et al. “Changes in Pedestrian and Bicyclist Injury Patterns in New York City After Adoption of Vision Zero.” JAMA Network Open. 2019;2(11):e1916703.
Citation B: Hartwell JR, Chen S, Kowalski PM, et al. “Longitudinal Effects of Road Diet Interventions on Pedestrian Mortality in Mid-Sized US Cities, 2010–2021.” American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 2023;64(3):412–419.


For each one, search PubMed or Google Scholar for the title, then the first author, then the journal plus volume and pages.
Check every field: does the article exist? Do the authors, journal, volume, and page numbers all match? If you find something, open the abstract and confirm the topic is actually what the citation describes.
Write down one sentence: what made the fabricated one convincing?

Expected result. Citation A is real (PMID 31783684). Citation B is fabricated—the authors, the specific title, and the volume and page numbers were invented. The journal is real; that article is not. You should be able to say what fooled you: a real journal, plausible author names, a reasonable topic for that journal, and correctly formatted volume and page numbers. That is precisely how AI fabrication works—it follows the pattern of a real citation, because the pattern is what it learned.
Check your work. If you concluded “B looks fine” from the formatting alone, that’s the lesson: a formatted citation is not a real one. The rule holds without exception—if you can’t open it and read the abstract, you can’t cite it. Fabricated references are the most common and most damaging AI error in academic work precisely because they look perfect.


Part B — Two of these numbers are wrong (~7 min)
No searching for this one. Everything you need is on the page. Below is a source fact sheet (treat it as the only ground truth) and an AI-generated summary of it. Both are fabricated for practice. Find the errors by hand.

SOURCE FACT SHEET
Philadelphia recorded 312 pedestrian crashes in 2023, resulting in 38 fatalities. 61% of crashes occurred after dark. 46% of all crashes were concentrated on the high-injury network, which makes up just 12% of city streets.


AI-GENERATED SUMMARY
In 2023, Philadelphia saw 312 pedestrian crashes and 38 deaths, a 24% increase over the previous year. 61% of crashes happened after dark, and 52% were concentrated on the high-injury network — just 12% of city streets.


Circle every number in the summary—there are six.
Take them one at a time and find each one in the fact sheet. Mark each VERIFIED or NOT IN SOURCE.
For anything you mark NOT IN SOURCE, decide which kind of problem it is: a number that was invented, or a number that was altered from a real one. They fail differently and are caught differently.

Expected result. Four verify: 312, 38, 61%, 12%. Two do not:

“24% increase” — invented. The fact sheet contains no year-over-year comparison at all. There is no previous-year figure anywhere in the source. This is the easier catch, because nothing like it exists to compare against.
“52%” — altered. The source says 46%. This is the dangerous one: a number in the right place, attached to the right claim, in a plausible range, differing from the truth by six points. A reader skimming for whether the summary “matches” will pass right over it.

Check your work. Did you catch 52%, or only 24%? Most people catch the invented number and miss the altered one—which is exactly backwards from the risk. Now notice what Part A would not have caught: every citation in a paragraph can be real and the prose around them can still be wrong. Verifying sources and verifying numbers are two separate jobs, and the second one has no shortcut. And a “not in source” flag starts your verification—it can also be a legitimate calculation or a rounding difference—it doesn’t finish it.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
section: Policy Orientation: What the Rules Actually Say (10 min)
text:
Policy Orientation: What the Rules Actually Say (10 min)
Ten minutes of orientation, not a policy reading. The point is to know when each rule binds you and where to look it up.
The line that runs through all four policies is the same one this series has held since Core 1: AI brainstorms and critiques; it does not draft your substantive scientific content. Brainstorm framings before you write, critique the draft after you write it—but the science, the feasibility, the citations, and the writing are yours.






ImportantThe four rules, condensed



NIH (NOT-OD-25-132, “Supporting Fairness and Originality in NIH Research Applications”): Applications “substantially developed by AI,” or containing sections substantially developed by AI, are not considered the applicant’s original ideas and will not be reviewed. NIH uses detection technology to identify AI-generated content, and if it’s discovered after an award, the matter can be referred to the Office of Research Integrity for a misconduct investigation—with possible consequences including disallowed costs, withheld future awards, suspension, and termination. The notice does allow AI “to assist in application preparation for limited aspects or in specific circumstances” (e.g., administrative tasks), but flags plagiarism and fabricated citations as risks. NIH does not require a disclosure form—its mechanism is prohibition plus detection. Separately, NIH peer reviewers are prohibited from using AI to write their critiques.
NSF (Notice to the Research Community on Use of Generative AI in the Merit Review Process): Proposers are asked to indicate in the project description the extent to which, if any, generative AI was used and how. You remain fully responsible for the accuracy and authenticity of everything submitted, including any AI-generated content—NSF’s existing fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism policies apply. NSF reviewers may not upload proposal content to non-approved AI tools.
ICMJE and COPE (ICMJE: AI Use by Authors · COPE: Authorship and AI Tools): AI cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work. Human authors are fully responsible for all content, including AI-assisted portions—you must review the output, verify it isn’t plagiarized, and confirm every citation is real. Disclose: ICMJE places disclosure in both the cover letter and the appropriate section of the manuscript; failing to disclose may require corrective action and can be construed as misconduct. COPE requires documenting transparently which tools were used, typically in methods or acknowledgments.
Peer review confidentiality is absolute. Never paste a manuscript you are reviewing into any AI tool. Many journals prohibit any AI use during review, not just uploading the text—check the reviewer guidelines before you touch a tool.
Everything else: foundation and journal policy is inconsistent and changing. Check the specific opportunity or the target journal’s author guidelines every single time. When policy is silent or unclear, disclose anyway.


Two contrasts worth holding on to. First, NIH and NSF are structurally different: NSF asks you to disclose, NIH tells you not to do it and looks for it. Disclosure does not make substantial AI drafting acceptable to NIH. Second, authorship and confidentiality are different rules that both apply: as an author you disclose your AI use; as a reviewer you keep the manuscript out of every tool. Neither one covers the other.
Longer worked examples of both workflows: Grant & Proposal Development and Manuscript Preparation & Peer Review.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
section: Activity 2: Write a Real Disclosure Statement
text:
Activity 2: Write a Real Disclosure Statement

Activity 2: Write a Real Disclosure Statement

Duration: ~12 minutes working time (13-minute slot) | Format: Write alone, then trade with a neighbor

Goal: Leave with one honest, specific disclosure statement written for a real piece of your own work—not a policy opinion about disclosure.

The worked example first (~3 min)
Here is the same disclosure written two ways. Read both before you write.
Too vague:

I used ChatGPT to help with this paper.

That tells a reader nothing they can act on. Which tool? For which parts? Did AI write the methods, or fix the commas? Was anything checked? A reader who cares about the answer still has to ask. A reader who doesn’t care wasn’t going to read it anyway. This sentence protects no one.
Specific and honest—two sentences:

I used ChatGPT Edu to brainstorm alternative framings for the significance section before drafting, and to critique the methods section after I had written it; all text in this manuscript was written by me. I verified every citation against the original article and every reported statistic against the source table, and I am responsible for the accuracy of all content, including the sections where AI provided feedback.

Notice what makes it work: it names the tool, it names what AI did and did not do (brainstormed and critiqued; did not draft), it names the verification step, and it ends with accountability. It’s two sentences. It took ninety seconds to write.
The calibration rule. Over-disclosing trivial use (spell-check, autocomplete, reformatting a table) is noise. Under-disclosing consequential use (drafting substance, shaping an argument, producing a number that ends up in a document) is a problem. Aim for where it matters to the reader.


Now write yours (~6 min)

Take the piece of your own work you brought—or, if you didn’t bring one, write the disclosure for something you did in Core 2 or Core 3, or for the AI-generated summary in Activity 1 above.
Write two sentences, no more, covering all four elements:

Tool — which one, named.
Scope — what AI did, and just as important, what it did not do.
Verification — what you personally checked, and against what.
Accountability — that the content is yours.

Decide where it goes: a methods or acknowledgments line, a cover-letter sentence, a footnote in a report, a line in an email, or—legitimately—nowhere, because the use was trivial. Write that decision down next to the statement.



Trade it (~3 min)
Hand your statement to a neighbor. Their only job is to answer one question: “After reading this, do I know what you actually did?” If they have to ask a follow-up, the statement isn’t specific enough yet. Fix it now, while someone is sitting there to tell you.
Expected result. A two-sentence disclosure that names a tool, distinguishes what AI did from what you did, states a verification step, and asserts your accountability—plus a decision about where it goes.
Check your work. Four tests, in order. (1) Could you delete your statement and lose nothing? Then it’s the vague version—rewrite it. (2) Does it name what AI did not do? That clause is what makes a disclosure informative rather than defensive. (3) Is the verification claim true? Never write “I verified every citation” unless you did—a false disclosure is worse than none. (4) Apply the funder and journal rules from the segment above: if this were an NIH application, would the scope you just described be allowable assistance or substantial development? If you had to think about it, that’s your answer—go and change the workflow, not the wording.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
text:
Activity 3: The Scrutiny Map

Activity 3: The Scrutiny Map

Duration: ~11 minutes working time (12-minute slot) | Format: Individual, then discuss the disagreements

Goal: Turn “use your judgment” into a decision you can defend on ten specific tasks.

The ten tasks
These are real DSPH work, spanning administrative, research, teaching, and student roles. Place each one in a scrutiny level—don’t skip the ones that feel obvious.

Admin. Draft a reminder email to committee members that their self-study section drafts are due Friday.
Admin. Turn messy department meeting notes into a recap circulated to the whole department.
Admin. Summarize a 40-page funding announcement into the one-page eligibility brief the team will use to decide whether to apply.
Research. Write the first draft of a Specific Aims page.
Research. Recode and clean a variable in an analysis dataset.
Research. Interpret a regression coefficient for the results section of a manuscript.
Research / community. Draft a plain-language summary of study findings for a community advisory board.
Teaching. Generate ten multiple-choice questions from this week’s assigned readings.
Teaching. Write a letter of recommendation for a doctoral student.
Student. Summarize thirty abstracts into a literature-review table for a qualifying exam.



The four scrutiny levels







Level
Means




Skim
Read the output once; errors are cheap and obvious


Spot-check
Verify a sample—one row, one claim, one calculation


Verify everything
Check every fact, number, and citation against its source before anyone acts on it


Don’t automate
A human does this; AI’s role at most is brainstorming or critique





Steps

For each of the ten, rate it quickly on three things: stakes (who is harmed if it’s wrong), reversibility (can you undo it), and verifiability (can you check it easily). Then assign one of the four levels. Six minutes—move fast, first instinct.
Pressure-test the map. Paste your ratings into ChatGPT Edu:

Here are ten tasks and the scrutiny level I assigned each, with my stakes/reversibility/verifiability ratings. Which did I likely mis-rate, and which deserve closer human scrutiny than I gave them? Argue the other side for my three most confident calls.

Find the person nearest you who placed a task differently and spend two minutes on why. The disagreements are the useful part.

Expected result. Ten tasks, each with a defensible scrutiny level, and at least one you moved after the pressure-test or the disagreement.
Check your work. Compare against these, and argue with them where you disagree—the reasoning matters more than matching:

#4 and #9 belong in “don’t automate.” The Specific Aims draft is squarely what NIH’s NOT-OD-25-132 prohibits—brainstorm and critique with AI, write it yourself. A recommendation letter is a judgment about a specific person that only you can make and that they can’t undo.
#3 and #6 belong in “verify everything.” Both are places where a confidently wrong sentence becomes a decision or a published claim, and both are cheap to check against a source you already have.
#5 belongs in “verify everything” even though it feels technical rather than consequential: a recoding error propagates silently into every result downstream and is close to invisible after the fact.
#2 is the trap. It scores low on stakes and looks like a skim—until you remember from Core 3 that department notes contain personnel asides, and “circulated to the whole department” is not reversible once it’s sent. Distribution changes the stakes, not the task.
#1, #8, and #10 are genuinely “skim” or “spot-check”—which is the point. The map’s job is to free your attention for the tasks that need it, not to make everything maximum-scrutiny.
#7 deserves more than it looks like it deserves. Plain-language rewriting is exactly where AI quietly changes what a finding means. Spot-check the claims, not the reading level.

Then the real test: would you defend your “skim” calls if one of them went wrong in public? The riskiest tasks usually feel routine.








TipGuard the skills you don’t want to lose



Handing thinking to a tool is fine in moderation—we all offload arithmetic to calculators. Too much erodes the very judgment you need to catch the tool’s mistakes, and your writing drifts toward a generic sameness. Aim for calibrated reliance: lean on AI for the low-stakes, reversible, checkable work you just mapped, and keep your hands on the rest. More on this in Keeping Your Judgment.

title: Core 4 · Verify, Disclose, Decide
section: Capstone: What You Can Now Do (5 min)
text:
Capstone: What You Can Now Do (5 min)
Not “what we covered.” What you personally did in the last fifty-five minutes:

You caught a fabricated citation. You have seen, first-hand, that a perfectly formatted reference in a real journal can be entirely invented—and you know the only defense: open it, or don’t cite it.
You caught a planted wrong number. Two of them, by hand, against a source—including the altered one that reads as plausible. You know that verifying sources and verifying numbers are different jobs.
You wrote one honest disclosure statement. Two sentences naming the tool, the scope, the verification, and your accountability—for a real piece of your own work, checked by a colleague who confirmed it says something.

That is the confidence move. You are not “being careful about AI” in the abstract. You have done the three things that make AI use defensible, on real material, and you can do them again tomorrow.
Take it with you. Put the two-sentence disclosure into the document it belongs to this week. Put the scrutiny map somewhere you’ll see it. And keep the rule that made all of it work: if you can’t open it, you can’t cite it.
